growth_story.headline: Mauritania's income per person is about where it was in 1968: oil and mining brought booms that faded, and a fast-growing population shares the gains.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, Mauritania's growth has run in two eras: income per person fell by 1.3 percent a year from 1990 to 2002, then rose by 1.4 percent a year from 2003 to 2025. The sources say little about the 1990s, and the World Bank links weak growth in the early 2000s to the global slowdown and bad weather. In the second era, oil production began in 2006 and income per person jumped 15.4 percent, but oil output fell within months and income per person declined every year from 2007 to 2010, through a military coup in 2008 and the global crisis. Oil, copper, gold and iron mining and a surge in public investment carried growth until commodity prices fell after 2014; since then growth has eased, with income per person rising 1.0 percent a year over 2016 to 2025 against 1.1 in the decade before. After falls in 2020 and 2021, income per person grew 3.7 percent in 2022 and in 2023 and 3.3 in 2024, then 1.2 in 2025 as extractive output contracted. In 2025 income per person was still 7.1 percent below its 1970 peak and about where it first was in 1968.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe two decades of resource-led growth that lifted Mauritania to lower-middle-income status, and strong growth in total output in 2024. Yet income per person in 2025 was about where it first was in 1968 and still below its 1970 peak, as a fast-growing population shares the gains and each boom has been followed by falls. The World Bank also puts growth in income per person in 2025 lower than the figures used here.
